title: Python
body:
The language this course is taught in, and the first one in the degree. Three decisions define
it, and every difference from [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2|C++]] traces back to one of
them.

## Interpreted, not compiled

[[Interpriting]] and [[Compiling]] already carry this: both routes end in
[[Machine Language]], but Python translates and executes at the same time instead of producing
an executable first. There is no `g++` step and no `a.out`.

```
hello.cpp  →  g++  →  a.out  →  run          C++: two steps, artifact in between
hello.py   →  python hello.py                Python: one step, no artifact
```

What that buys is the interactive prompt and a fast edit-run cycle, which is most of why a first
course uses it. What it costs is stated in `Interpriting.md`: the source has to be on the machine
every time, and it is slower, because translation happens again on every run rather than once.

## Dynamically typed

**A [[Variable]] in C has a type; in Python the *value* has a type and the variable is just a
name.** No declaration, no type in the source, and a name can be rebound to a different type:

```python
x = 5        # x names an int
x = "five"   # now it names a str. Legal.
```

```c
int x = 5;
x = "five";  /* compile error, and that is the point */
```

This is the single biggest practical difference and it changes when you find out you are wrong.
It does **not** mean Python has no types: `5 + "five"` is a `TypeError`, it just arrives at run
time. See [[Data type]] and [[Type casting]].

| | C / C++ | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Types declared | yes, in the source | no |
| Type checked | compile time | run time, at the operation |
| A name can change type | no | yes |
| Wrong type found | before you run it | when that line executes, maybe never |

## Indentation is syntax

Braces do not delimit blocks; the indentation does. A misaligned line is not a style problem, it
is a different program or a `SyntaxError`. This is why block 2's [[Style Conventions]] are graded
in this course and treated as taste in others: here the layout **is** the code.

## What this does to errors

The [[Errors]] taxonomy transfers, with one real change. C's [[Compile Errors]] are caught by a
step Python does not have, so:

- **Syntax errors** still arrive before anything runs, raised by the parser when the file is read.
- **Type mismatches**, which C catches at compile time, become [[Runtime Errors]] here. A branch
  that never executes never reports its type error at all.
- **[[Logic Errors]]** are identical in both languages, because no language catches those.

That third row is why [[Test Coverage]] matters more in a dynamically typed language, not less:
the compiler is not covering the easy half for you.

## Core facts

- Interpreted: translated and executed together, no separate build artifact.
- Dynamically typed: values carry types, names do not, and checking happens at run time.
- Strongly typed as well as dynamically typed: `5 + "five"` fails, it does not silently coerce.
- Indentation delimits blocks, so whitespace is syntax.
- `input()` always returns a [[String]]; converting it is the first real bug most people hit.
- Everything is an object, including functions, which is where [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] picks up.
- The standard library is large and shipped ([[Standard Library]]), which is why a first course
  can do graphics in week three.
